q: What distinguishes sarcopenia from an isolated finding of low muscle mass?
o: Equating every case with physical frailty
Defining the condition solely by a low muscle-mass estimate
Equating every case with inflammatory cachexia
Incorporating muscle function, rather than muscle mass alone
explanation:
The chapter describes sarcopenia as involving low muscle function and stresses the limitations of mass alone (p732).

B. Defining the condition solely by a low muscle-mass estimate: The chapter describes unreliable mass estimates and poor correlation with relevant outcomes (p732).
C. Equating every case with inflammatory cachexia: Cachexia has a distinct catabolic/inflammatory pathophysiology and may coexist with sarcopenia (p736).
A. Equating every case with physical frailty: The constructs overlap, but mild sarcopenia need not cause frailty and frailty may have nonmuscular causes (p736).

q: Why is a bedside BIA result less definitive than a direct measurement of muscle function?
o: It directly measures the SPPB balance and chair-stand components
It estimates mass using population- and device-specific equations and cutoffs
explanation:
BIA is useful at the bedside, but its population- and device-specific equations and cutoffs lack standardization and limit accuracy (p735); mass estimates have weaker links to outcomes (p732).

D. It directly measures grip strength: Grip is a strength measurement; BIA estimates muscle mass (p735).
C. It directly measures gait speed: Gait speed is a physical-performance measure; BIA estimates mass (p735).
A. It directly measures the SPPB balance and chair-stand components: Those components belong to physical-performance assessment; BIA instead estimates mass (p735).

q: A person has low muscle mass, preserved gait/grip, and low food intake without a catabolic disease. Which diagnosis does this chapter prioritize?
explanation:
When low muscle mass is not accompanied by low muscle function, the chapter prioritizes malnutrition as the main diagnosis (p736).

D. Sarcopenia: Preserved grip and gait do not supply the low-function component; the chapter prioritizes malnutrition in this pattern (p736).
C. Cachexia: The chapter describes disease-associated wasting with excess catabolism and inflammation, absent from the stem (p736).
B. Physical frailty: The physical frailty construct includes weakness and slowness; isolated low mass with preserved function does not establish it (p736).
